extracted.intended_audience: general readers and YouTube users/creators seeking an overview of the platform, its features, and its policies
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic overview of YouTube's features, product tiers, legal and policy frameworks, content moderation/enforcement practices, and creator-facing requirements. Useful for readers who want to understand what the platform allows, restricts, or enforces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature access and verification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is optional; however certain tasks require an account (uploading videos, viewing flagged (18+) videos, creating playlists, liking/disliking, posting comments). Verification via phone number or channel history increases feature availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouTube groups features into tiers: basic/standard (uploading, playlists, YouTube Music use with limits), intermediate (longer videos — historically >15 minutes —, live streaming, custom thumbnails, creating podcasts) and advanced (content ID appeals, embedding live streams, applying for monetization, clickable links, adding chapters, pinning comments). Verification (phone number or channel history) or meeting other eligibility conditions is required to unlock intermediate/advanced features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright takedown (DMCA) and three-strike consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube does not pre-screen uploads; it relies on copyright holders to issue DMCA takedown notices pursuant to the Online Copyright Infringement Liability Limitation Act. Any successful complaint about copyright infringement results in a YouTube copyright strike; three successful complaints for copyright infringement against a user account will result in the account and all of its uploaded videos being deleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At upload users are shown a message asking them not to violate copyright laws. The platform's reliance on rights-holder notices (rather than pre-moderation) is a core procedural rule that determines enforcement timing and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content ID automated detection and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Content ID creates an ID file for copyrighted audio/video material and stores it in a database. When an uploaded video matches Content ID, it flags the video and the content owner can choose to block the video, track its viewing statistics, or add advertisements to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content ID is an automated system; its use to remove material without human review has been controversial, especially where fair use might apply. There is a dispute process: before 2016 videos were not monetized until disputes resolved; since April 2016 videos in dispute continue to be monetized and the money goes to whoever wins the dispute. Uploaders can remove disputed audio to try to monetize again. Content ID effectiveness varies and is not infallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use requirement before takedown (Lenz precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lenz v. Universal Music Corp. (2008) held that copyright holders cannot order the removal of an online file without first determining whether the posting reflected fair use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require rights-holders to consider fair use before issuing takedowns; Google/YouTube has stated it will help cover legal costs in select cases where it believes fair use defenses apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization, demonetization, and revenue enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetization on YouTube (ads, Premium, channel subscriptions, Super Chat, etc.) is subject to content and rights enforcement: creators have had videos taken down or demonetized when Content ID or other systems identify copyrighted material, even for short segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement and monetization outcomes can differ by rights-holder/record label. Content ID choices by rights-holders (block/track/monetize) directly affect whether the uploader can earn revenue. YouTube's monetization programs and policy choices change over time and interact with dispute and Content ID outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPPA compliance and 'made for kids' designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a COPPA-related complaint, YouTube was fined $170 million and ordered to create systems to increase children's privacy. From January 6, 2020, YouTube started treating all videos designated as 'made for kids' as liable under COPPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouTube implemented platform-level changes (treating 'made for kids' content under stricter rules), introduced YouTube Kids with curated content and parental controls, and added a supervised mode for tweens. Creators must correctly designate child-directed content to comply with COPPA-related rules and privacy protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy against clickbait/misleading titles (Dec 2024 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube announced guidelines prohibiting videos with clickbait titles to enhance content quality and combat misinformation. The platform aims to penalize creators using misleading or sensationalized titles, with potential actions including video removal or channel suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new enforcement was to roll out in India first and expand to other countries over time. This is a content-quality policy tied to title/metadata rather than solely to video content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of public dislike counts and visibility policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In November 2021 YouTube removed public dislike counts on videos, stating that the change reduced dislike attacks and brigading. Creators can still see like/dislike counts in YouTube Studio; viewers cannot. Third-party tools (e.g., Return YouTube Dislike) exist to surface dislikes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision was defended by YouTube leadership as anti-harassment; it was criticized by some (including a co-founder) as reducing crowd-sourced signals of quality. The policy change shows trade-offs between community signaling and harassment mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age assurance and verification policies
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube/Google announced trials to enforce 'age assurance' policies (in response to the UK Online Safety Act) using machine learning to estimate user age. If a user is assumed to be a minor, access to certain features can be restricted and the user must pass age verification (payment, scanned ID, or selfie) to access full features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For presumed minors, personalized advertising may be disabled and certain digital wellbeing limits enabled. This policy affects which content/features a user may see or use and imposes verification workflows for disputed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad-blocker enforcement and server-side ad injection
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube cracked down on the use of ad blockers: users of ad blockers may see pop-up warnings and could be blocked after limited viewing; YouTube considers ad-blocker use a violation of its Terms of Service. The platform started using server-side ad injection to integrate ads directly into video streams, undermining typical ad-blocker techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader changes in browser extension frameworks (e.g., Chrome's Manifest V3) and server-side approaches reduce the effectiveness of third-party ad-blockers and change enforcement mechanics against ad-blocking users and third-party apps.

rubrics_metrics.name: View-count and subscriber-count integrity rules
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube's Terms forbid automated processes to inflate view counts. The platform has removed suspicious views (e.g., 2012 removal of two billion views) and patched historic anomalies (e.g., the '301' freeze). Since September 2019 subscriber counts are abbreviated publicly; exact counts remain available to channel operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouTube monitors and corrects view/subscriber metrics to preserve integrity; public display policies (abbreviations) can reduce third-party real-time tracking but channel owners retain detailed analytics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content moderation enforcement (channel removals, suspensions, jurisdictional actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube enforces its policies by removing channels, deleting accounts, suspending creators, and complying with local legal orders. Examples include removal of channels linked to state media for breaching policies, deletion of channels for COVID-19 policy violations, and court-ordered fines/decisions in various jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement steps include removal of channels, policy-based suspensions, and region-specific actions; outcomes can be contested and have political/legal implications. Platform decisions (e.g., reinstating creators) may shift over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Kids content curation and parental controls
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube Kids is a separate app designed for children with curated channel selections, parental control features, and filtering of videos deemed inappropriate for children under chosen age groupings (under 13, 8, or 5 depending on settings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The app provides age-based interfaces, curated content, and parental controls; it is rolled out across many countries and has both mobile and web versions. The product is a platform-level mitigation tied to child-safety and content suitability rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upload length/size and account eligibility history
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, early YouTube uploads were limited (e.g., 100 MB, ~30 seconds). Over time platform rules changed (e.g., December 2010 changes allowing some users to upload videos of unlimited length) and eligibility for longer uploads or other features depends on account verification/standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upload limits and eligibility are operational rules that govern what creators can publish; they have evolved and depend on verification and other account-level criteria.
